title: How Flesh-eating Bacteria Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain flesh-eating bacteria (necrotizing fasciitis), using the case of Amy Copeland, a 24-year-old Georgia woman who fell on a zip line into brackish water and developed the infection through a leg gash. They describe how Aeromonas hydrophila and group A strep produce toxins that trigger an overwhelming, destructive immune response (cytokines, macrophages, free radicals), how the infection spreads through fascia, and how it can lead to toxic shock syndrome. They cover the rapid progression and timeline, treatment (antibiotics, immunoglobulin, debridement, amputation, skin grafts), historical naming during the Civil War and Fournier's gangrene, the tampon link to toxic shock, warning signs, wound-care and hygiene advice, risk factors (recent infection, cuts, steroids, diabetes, black tar heroin use), and prevention. The episode ends with a fundraising mention for Amy Copeland and listener mail about a shrunken head.

segments.title: Opening banter and Amy Copeland introduction
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the sidebar and note flesh-eating bacteria is rare (about five cases a year). They introduce Amy Copeland, who fell from a zip line into brackish water and got infected through a leg gash.

segments.title: How the bacteria attack the body
segments.summary: Explanation of how Aeromonas hydrophila and strep bacteria enter through wounds, produce cytotoxins and exotoxins, and trigger an overwhelming immune response with cytokines, macrophages and free radicals that destroy tissue.

segments.title: Spread through fascia and speed of progression
segments.summary: The infection spreads through fascia, the connective membrane beneath the skin, destroying tissue; it can progress from a small wound to life-threatening within days, as with a Tulsa football player who died in a week. Toxic shock syndrome is mentioned as a complication.

segments.title: Amy Copeland's treatment and other cases
segments.summary: Amy Copeland had her left leg, right foot, both hands and part of her torso amputated and later skin grafts. Another Cartersville, Georgia patient was treated in the room next to hers at a burn center in Augusta. Treatment includes high-dose antibiotics, immunoglobulin, debridement and amputation if needed.

segments.title: Symptoms, stages and toxic shock syndrome history
segments.summary: Describes the progression over days: swelling, purple rash, blisters, skin peeling, then toxic shock around days four to five. Discusses the early association of toxic shock syndrome with high-absorbency tampons and why it is now understood as an infection-driven immune reaction.

segments.title: Wound care, risk factors and prevention
segments.summary: Advice on cleaning wounds with cold water and soap around the wound, using alcohol-cleaned tweezers, and asking a doctor about bandaging. Risk factors include recent infection, cuts, steroids, diabetes and black tar heroin use. Hand washing and avoiding recontamination in public bathrooms are recommended.

segments.title: Naming history and Civil War origins
segments.summary: The condition was known since the Civil War and named by location, such as Fournier's gangrene for the genitals and Ludwig's angina for the head and neck. It was later classified by bacteria type and the term necrotizing fasciitis was adopted in 1952; the first described was a Confederate surgeon named Joseph Jones.

segments.title: Amy Copeland donations and listener mail
segments.summary: Hosts mention donation site for Amy Copeland and read listener mail from Mike Keys in Limerick, Ireland, about walking his dogs and owning a shrunken head.

segments.title: Sign-off and topic requests
segments.summary: Hosts invite topic requests via Twitter, Facebook and email, and close the episode.
